did_you_know.text: The verb "ויחוגו" is related to the word "חג" (festival). In the Bible, a festival is not only a date on the calendar but also a gathering and celebration before God.
"Pharaoh" was not the king’s personal name but a royal title derived from the Egyptian expression "the Great House." Only later did it become the usual word for the ruler of Egypt.

"Hebrews" is an ancient designation for the Israelites, alongside the term "Children of Israel." Scholars sometimes compare it with the ancient term "Habiru," but there is no agreement that the two are exactly the same.
In ancient times, bricks were often made from mud mixed with straw or other plant fibers. The fibers helped strengthen the bricks and reduce cracking as the mud dried.
Here, the word "quota" refers to a fixed amount of production, not merely a shape or pattern. The workers’ target stayed the same even though they now had to gather the raw material themselves.

In the Bible, "שוטרים" does not mean only police officers in the modern sense; it can mean officials or supervisors. In this chapter, they are Israelites expected to oversee the workers and report on their labor.
The phrase "you have made us smell bad" is a metaphor. It refers not to a real odor but to damaging their reputation and standing before Pharaoh.
Moses does not hide his difficult question; he brings it directly to God. In the Bible, prayer can include complaint, pain, and a demand for understanding—not only praise and thanks.
